title: Planning a Small Farm Business
summary: Students learn how to create a simple budget, research local markets, and keep basic records for a small farm. They finish with a clear plan they could start using right away.
objectives: Create a basic farm budget using estimated costs and income
Identify at least two local markets for selling farm products
Collect and organize simple farm records such as expenses and yields
Compare different pricing options to choose a realistic selling price
Write a one‑page farm business plan that includes budget, market, and record‑keeping
prerequisites: Students should already know basic plant needs, soil basics, and why crop rotation matters from earlier lessons.
why: Running a farm is like running any small business: you need to know how much money goes in and out, who will buy your products, and how to track performance. Without these skills, a farm can quickly run out of money or miss opportunities to sell at a good price.

Good budgeting, market research, and record‑keeping also help farmers make decisions that protect the environment and their community. When you know what works financially, you can choose sustainable practices that keep the land healthy for years to come.

sections.heading: 1. Why a Farm Needs a Budget
sections.body:
A farm, even a small one, is a tiny business.  
Just like a shop or a school project, it needs a plan for how much money will come in and how much will go out. That plan is called a **budget**.

> **Definition:** A budget is a written estimate of all the money you expect to spend and all the money you expect to earn over a set period of time (usually a season or a year).

### Why a budget matters

1. **It tells you what you can afford.**  
   If you know you will need $200 for seeds, $150 for tools, $100 for water, and $250 for labor, you can add those numbers up and see whether you have enough cash or need a loan.  

2. **It prevents surprise costs.**  
   Imagine you buy seeds and later discover you need extra fertilizer that you didn’t think about. Without a budget, that extra $80 would cut into your profit or force you to borrow money at the last minute.  

3. **It helps you set realistic goals.**  
   When you know your total expected costs, you can decide how much you need to sell to make a profit. This keeps you from hoping for a huge profit that is actually impossible.

### Simple categories for a small farm budget

| Category | What it includes | Example cost |
|----------|------------------|--------------|
| **Seeds** | Packets of vegetable or grain seeds | $30 |
| **Tools** | Hand tools, small tractor rental, repair parts | $120 |
| **Water** | Irrigation pumps, electricity or fuel for pumps | $80 |
| **Labor** | Your own time (if you count it), hired help | $200 |
| **Sales** | Money you expect to receive from customers | $800 |

You can write these categories on a piece of paper or in a spreadsheet. Then fill in the numbers you expect for each item. The total expected cost is the sum of the first four columns:

$$\text{Total Cost} = \text{Seeds} + \text{Tools} + \text{Water} + \text{Labor}$$

If you expect to earn $800 from sales, the profit you hope for is:

$$\text{Profit} = \text{Sales} - \text{Total Cost}$$

### How a budget avoids surprises

Think of a budget like a road map for a trip. Before you leave home, you check how much fuel you need, whether the car is in good shape, and where you will stop for food. If you skip the map, you might run out of gas in the middle of nowhere.  

Similarly, a farm budget shows you where money will be needed **before** you actually need it. If you notice that water costs are higher than you thought, you can look for cheaper irrigation methods early, rather than paying a big bill after the crops have already been watered.

> **In daily life:** When you plan a birthday party, you list the cost of the cake, decorations, and gifts. That list is a mini‑budget and helps you avoid spending more than you have.

### A quick step‑by‑step to make your first budget

1. **List every expense** you can think of, even small ones like a bag of fertilizer.  
2. **Assign a realistic price** to each item. Use receipts from previous years or ask local suppliers for quotes.  
3. **Add them up** to get your total expected cost.  
4. **Estimate your income** by thinking about how many kilograms of produce you will sell and at what price.  
5. **Subtract** the total cost from the estimated income. If the result is positive, you have a profit; if it is negative, you need to either cut costs or raise prices.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to include “hidden” costs such as transportation of produce to market or the cost of your own time. These can turn a seemingly profitable plan into a loss.

### Keep it simple

You do not need a complex spreadsheet right away. A notebook with five rows (one for each category) and two columns (expected cost and actual cost) is enough to start. As you gain experience, you can add more detail, like separate rows for different seed varieties or for marketing expenses.

> **Remember:** A budget is a living document. Update the “actual cost” column as you spend money, and compare it to the “expected cost” column. This habit will show you where you were right and where you need to improve next season.

By making a budget, you give your small farm a clear financial picture. That picture guides your decisions, protects you from unexpected expenses, and increases the chance that your farm will be both productive and profitable.

sections.heading: 2. Estimating Costs and Income
sections.body:
Imagine you are planning a small garden that will later become a tiny farm. Before you buy seeds, tools, or even water, you need to know **how much money you will spend** and **how much money you might earn**. This is called *estimating costs and income*.  

> **Definition:** *Estimating* means making a careful guess based on the information you have.  

Why do we estimate?  
If you spend more than you earn, the farm will lose money and you may have to stop. If you earn more than you spend, you can keep the farm running, buy better equipment, or save for the future. Think of it like a school project: you list the materials you need (paper, glue, paint) and then check how many points the project is worth. You only start the project if the points are worth the effort and cost.

### Step 1: List Every Possible Expense  

Write down every thing you will have to pay for. Use a simple table on paper or a spreadsheet. Below is a sample table you can copy:

| Item                     | Quantity | Cost per unit ($) | Total cost ($) |
|--------------------------|----------|-------------------|----------------|
| Seeds (tomatoes)         | 5 packs  | 3.00              | =5×3 = 15.00   |
| Seedlings (lettuce)      | 20 pcs   | 0.50              | =20×0.5 = 10.00|
| Fertiliser (bag)         | 2 bags   | 12.00             | =2×12 = 24.00 |
| Irrigation tubing (m)    | 30 m     | 0.80              | =30×0.8 = 24.00|
| Tools (hand trowel)      | 1 set    | 15.00             | =1×15 = 15.00 |
| Water (monthly bill)     | 3 months | 25.00             | =3×25 = 75.00 |
| **Total Expenses**       |          |                   | **$163.00**   |

**How to fill the table**

1. **Item** – what you are buying.  
2. **Quantity** – how many you need.  
3. **Cost per unit** – price of one piece or one kilogram.  
4. **Total cost** – multiply quantity by cost per unit.  

The multiplication is written as an *equation*:  

$$\text{Total cost} = \text{Quantity} \times \text{Cost per unit}$$  

Do this for every line. Add all the total‑cost numbers at the bottom to get your *total expenses*.

> **Note:** Always add a small extra amount (5‑10 %) for unexpected costs, like a broken tool or a sudden pest problem.  

### Step 2: Estimate Your Income  

Now think about what you will sell and how much you can earn. Use a similar table:

| Crop          | Expected yield (kg) | Sale price per kg ($) | Expected income ($) |
|---------------|---------------------|-----------------------|---------------------|
| Tomatoes      | 80 kg               | 2.00                  | =80×2 = 160.00      |
| Lettuce       | 30 kg               | 1.50                  | =30×1.5 = 45.00     |
| **Total Income** |                 |                       | **$205.00**         |

**How to estimate yield**

- Look up average yields for your region (e.g., a tomato plant often gives 10 kg per season).  
- Multiply the number of plants by that average.  

**How to set a sale price**

- Check local market prices or ask neighbours.  
- Choose a price that covers your costs and gives a small profit.

The income equation looks the same as the cost equation:

$$\text{Expected income} = \text{Yield} \times \text{Sale price per unit}$$  

Add all the expected‑income numbers to get the *total income*.

> **In daily life:** This is like estimating how much money you will make from a lemonade stand: count how many cups you can sell, decide the price per cup, then multiply.

### Step 3: Compare Costs and Income  

Subtract total expenses from total income to see if you will make a profit.

$$\text{Profit} = \text{Total Income} - \text{Total Expenses}$$  

Using the sample numbers:  

$$\text{Profit} = 205.00 - 163.00 = 42.00$$  

A positive profit ($42) means the farm could be viable, but the margin is small. You might look for ways to lower costs (cheaper water source) or increase income (sell a higher‑value variety).

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to count recurring costs such as water or fertilizer each month. This makes the profit look larger than it really is.

### Step 4: Check Your Assumptions  

Ask yourself:

- Are the yield numbers realistic for my soil and climate?  
- Did I include labor time (even if it’s my own work)?  
- What if the market price drops by $0.20 per kg?  

You can make a *what‑if* table by changing one number at a time and recalculating profit. This simple test shows how sensitive your farm is to changes.

### Quick Checklist  

- List every expense, multiply quantity × unit cost.  
- List every crop, estimate yield, multiply yield × sale price.  
- Add totals, subtract to find profit.  
- Add a safety margin (5‑10 %) for unexpected costs.  
- Test a few “what‑if” scenarios.

When you finish these steps, you have a clear picture of the money side of your small farm. This knowledge will guide decisions about what to plant, how much to invest, and whether you need extra help or a bigger market.

sections.heading: 3. Finding Your Market
sections.body:
Imagine you are opening a tiny shop on the corner of your street. Before you buy any shelves or stock, you would first ask: *Who will walk by and want to buy what I am selling?* The same question is the first step for a small farm. **Finding your market** means discovering the people who are ready to purchase the vegetables, eggs, or honey you plan to grow.  

### 1. What is a “market”?

> **Definition:** *Market* – a group of customers who might buy a product, and the place (physical or online) where the buying happens.

A market is not just a building; it is the collection of buyers and the way they find what they need. Knowing your market helps you avoid growing a crop that no one wants, saving time, land, and money.

### 2. Identify nearby markets

Start by making a simple list of all the possible places where you could sell your farm products. These might include:

- A weekly farmers’ market in town  
- The grocery store on Main Street  
- A local restaurant that uses fresh produce  
- A community‑supported agriculture (CSA) program where families pay for a share of the harvest  
- Direct sales from your farm gate (a “farm stand”)  

Write each option on a separate line and add a column for *distance* (how far it is from your farm) and *opening days*. This small table gives you a visual picture of what is close enough for a small operation.

### 3. Talk to potential buyers

Now that you have a list, reach out. You do not need a fancy survey; a short conversation works well.

- **Farmers’ market organizer:** Ask about stall fees, the typical number of visitors, and what products are already being sold.  
- **Grocery store manager:** Inquire whether they accept small local suppliers, what quantity they need each week, and how they handle payments.  
- **Restaurant chef:** Find out which vegetables or herbs they use most, and whether they prefer organic or locally‑grown items.  

When you speak, note down two things:

1. **Price range** – the typical price per kilogram or per dozen that buyers pay.  
2. **Requirements** – minimum order size, delivery schedule, or certification (e.g., organic).  

### 4. Note prices and compare

Collect the price information in a simple table:

| Market | Typical price ($/kg) | Minimum order | Notes |
|--------|---------------------|---------------|-------|
| Farmers’ market | 2.50 | 5 kg | Cash only, stall $10/day |
| Grocery store | 2.20 | 20 kg | Weekly delivery, check payment |
| Restaurant | 2.80 | 10 kg | Prefers organic, pays on receipt |
| CSA | 2.00 | 1 share (≈15 kg) | Subscription model |

Having the numbers side‑by‑side lets you see which market pays the most per kilogram and which has the lowest entry barrier.  

> **Note:** The *best* market is not always the one with the highest price. Consider how much you can realistically produce and how much effort is needed to meet the buyer’s rules.

### 5. Choose the best fit for your farm’s size and products

Now ask yourself three questions:

1. **Can I meet the minimum order?** If you only have 30 kg of carrots this season, a market that demands 50 kg each week is not a good match.  
2. **Is the distance manageable?** Driving 30 km to a grocery store every week adds fuel cost and time, which reduces profit.  
3. **Do the product requirements match what I grow?** If a restaurant only wants organic lettuce and you do not have certification, you may need extra steps that cost more than the price advantage.

Select one or two markets that satisfy all three questions. Many small farms start with a **farm stand** and a **farmers’ market stall** because they have low entry costs and let the farmer interact directly with customers, building trust and repeat sales.

### 6. Quick check – a simple equation

To see whether a market will be profitable, you can use the basic profit formula:

$$
\text{Profit} = (\text{Price per unit} \times \text{Quantity sold}) - \text{Total cost}
$$

If the profit is positive and large enough to cover your time and future investments, the market is a good candidate.

> **In daily life:** Think of this like deciding whether to sell homemade cookies at school. You count how much you charge per cookie, how many you can bake, and the cost of flour and sugar. If you make more money than you spend, you’ve found a good “market” for your cookies.

### 7. Summarise your findings

Write a short paragraph for each market you considered, stating:

- What you learned about price and requirements  
- Why it is or isn’t a good fit for your farm size  
- The next step (e.g., “Apply for a stall at the farmers’ market for the spring season.”)

Having this written plan makes the next stage—setting prices and budgeting—much clearer.

> **Remember:** Market research is a one‑time start‑up activity, but you should revisit it each season. Prices, buyer needs, and your own farm capacity can change, and staying informed keeps your small farm business healthy.

sections.heading: 4. Setting Prices
sections.body:
When you decide how much to charge for the vegetables, eggs, or honey you grow, the first thing you must do is make sure the price is **high enough to pay all your costs** and still leave a little money left over – that extra money is your profit.

> **Definition:** *Profit* is the amount of money left after you have paid every expense needed to run your farm. It is the reward for the work you put in and the risk you take.

### 1. Start with the total cost per unit  

Take the budget you created in the earlier lesson and look at the **total cost** for the product you are selling. Total cost includes:

* **Fixed costs** – money you spend even if you produce nothing, such as land rent, tools, or a small loan payment.  
* **Variable costs** – money that changes with how much you produce, such as seeds, feed, fertilizer, water, and labor.

Add these two groups together to get the **total cost** for the whole harvest. Then divide that number by the number of units you expect to sell (for example, 200 heads of lettuce). The result is the **cost per unit**.

$$
\text{Cost per unit} = \frac{\text{Fixed costs} + \text{Variable costs}}{\text{Number of units expected to sell}}
$$

If your fixed costs are \$120, variable costs are \$180, and you plan to sell 300 tomatoes, the calculation is:

$$
\text{Cost per unit} = \frac{120 + 180}{300} = \frac{300}{300} = \$1.00
$$

### 2. Add a small profit margin  

A **profit margin** is a percentage of the cost that you add to make a profit. For a small starter farm, a margin of 10 %–20 % is often enough to cover unexpected expenses and give you a modest reward.

To add a 15 % margin, multiply the cost per unit by 1 + margin (where the margin is written as a decimal).

$$
\text{Selling price} = \text{Cost per unit} \times (1 + \text{Margin})
$$

Using the tomato example above with a 15 % margin:

$$
\text{Selling price} = 1.00 \times (1 + 0.15) = 1.00 \times 1.15 = \$1.15
$$

Now each tomato should be sold for at least \$1.15 to cover costs and give you a small profit.

> **In daily life:** Think of a lemonade stand. If you spend \$0.30 on lemons and sugar for each cup and want a little extra for your effort, you might add a 20 % margin, making the price \$0.36. You would probably round up to \$0.40 because customers find whole‑dollar or whole‑cent prices easier to understand.

### 3. Check the market price  

Your calculated selling price must also be realistic compared to what other sellers charge. Look at the **market price** – the price that nearby farms, grocery stores, or farmers’ markets are asking for the same product.

* If your price is **much higher** than the market price, customers may buy elsewhere.  
* If your price is **much lower**, you might be missing out on profit or even losing money if the market price is still above your cost.

Suppose the local market sells tomatoes for \$1.30 each. Your calculated price of \$1.15 is lower, which could attract buyers while still giving you profit. If the market price were only \$0.90, you would need to reconsider either your costs (maybe find cheaper seeds) or accept a smaller margin.

> **Common mistake:** Adding profit *after* looking at the market price instead of before. If you first see the market price and then add profit, you may end up with a price that does not cover your actual costs.

### 4. Adjust for special factors  

Sometimes you can charge a little more because of:

* **Quality** – organic or heirloom varieties often fetch higher prices.  
* **Convenience** – delivering directly to a restaurant or a school may allow a premium.  
* **Seasonality** – a product that is scarce in winter can be priced higher.

If any of these apply, you can increase the margin slightly (for example, from 15 % to 20 %). Just be sure the new price still feels reasonable to your customers.

### 5. Write the price into your mini business plan  

In the “Putting It All Together” section you will list each product, its cost per unit, the chosen profit margin, and the final selling price. This makes it easy to see at a glance whether your farm will be financially viable.

> **Remember:** The selling price must (1) cover every cost, (2) include a profit margin, and (3) be competitive with the market. If any one of these three parts is missing, the farm may struggle to stay afloat.

sections.heading: 5. Simple Record‑Keeping
sections.body:
A simple record‑keeping system is like a diary for your farm.  
Each day you write down what you did, how much it cost or earned, and how much you produced.  
When the numbers are already written in the same place, adding them up later is quick and almost error‑free.

**Why daily notes help**

Think of a school notebook where you write every homework assignment as soon as it is given.  
At the end of the term you can easily count how many assignments you completed and see which subjects needed more work.  
If you waited until the end of the term to remember everything, you would have to guess or search through memory, and you would likely miss some tasks. The same idea works for a farm: writing each transaction as it happens removes the need to rely on memory.

### The basic log format

Create a table with four columns. You can draw it on paper, use a spreadsheet, or a simple note‑taking app. The columns are:

| Date | Activity | Amount ($) | Quantity |
|------|----------|------------|----------|

* **Date** – the calendar day (e.g., 2026‑09‑15).  
* **Activity** – what you did: planting, buying seed, selling lettuce, fixing a fence, etc.  
* **Amount** – money spent (enter a negative number) or money earned (enter a positive number).  
* **Quantity** – how much you produced or used, measured in the unit that makes sense for that item (kilograms of tomatoes, number of chickens, hours of labor, etc.).

When you fill in a line, you are recording a single event. For example:

| 2026‑09‑15 | Bought tomato seed | -12.50 | 5 kg |
| 2026‑09‑16 | Planted tomatoes   | 0.00  | 20 plants |
| 2026‑09‑20 | Sold tomatoes      | 45.00 | 15 kg |

> **Note:** Use a minus sign (‑) for any cost. This lets you add the whole column later without having to remember which rows are expenses and which are income.

### Turning the log into useful totals

Once you have several days of entries, you can calculate totals with very simple arithmetic.

The total money spent (costs) is the sum of all negative amounts:

$$\text{Total Cost} = \sum_{\text{rows}} \text{Amount}_{\text{negative}}$$

The total money earned (revenue) is the sum of all positive amounts:

$$\text{Total Revenue} = \sum_{\text{rows}} \text{Amount}_{\text{positive}}$$

Your profit for the period is simply:

$$\text{Profit} = \text{Total Revenue} - \text{Total Cost}$$

Because the numbers are already separated by sign, you can use the same column for both calculations. Most spreadsheet programs have a built‑in “SUMIF” function that does exactly this.

### How the quantity column helps

The quantity column lets you see how efficiently you are using resources. Suppose you bought 5 kg of seed for $12.50 and later harvested 15 kg of tomatoes. You can compute a yield ratio:

$$\text{Yield Ratio} = \frac{\text{Quantity Produced}}{\text{Quantity Purchased}} = \frac{15\text{ kg}}{5\text{ kg}} = 3$$

A ratio greater than 1 means you produced more than you bought, which is a good sign. If the ratio is close to 1, you may need to improve growing techniques.

> **In daily life:** Farmers who keep a daily log can answer questions like “How much did I spend on feed last month?” or “What was my profit from the strawberry patch in June?” with a quick glance at the table, just as a shopper can check a receipt to see how much they spent on groceries.

### Tips for staying consistent

1. **Write every transaction the same day** – even a quick note on your phone is fine.  
2. **Use the same units** – if you measure tomatoes in kilograms, keep using kilograms; don’t switch to pounds halfway through.  
3. **Review weekly** – at the end of each week, add up the columns and note any surprising numbers. This habit catches mistakes early.

> **Common mistake:** Skipping days because “nothing happened.” Even a day with no money change is worth noting: write “0” in the Amount column and describe the activity (e.g., “Weeds removed”). This prevents gaps that make later calculations confusing.

### Quick example of a weekly summary

| Date | Activity            | Amount ($) | Quantity |
|------|---------------------|------------|----------|
| 2026‑09‑01 | Bought chick feed | -20.00 | 10 kg |
| 2026‑09‑02 | Fed chickens       | 0.00   | 5 kg |
| 2026‑09‑03 | Collected eggs     | 15.00  | 30 eggs |
| 2026‑09‑04 | Sold eggs          | 30.00  | 30 eggs |
| 2026‑09‑05 | Vet check          | -45.00 | 0 |
| 2026‑09‑06 | No activity        | 0.00   | 0 |

Weekly totals:  
*Total Cost* = –20.00 – 45.00 = **‑65.00**  
*Total Revenue* = 15.00 + 30.00 = **45.00**  
*Profit* = 45.00 – 65.00 = **‑20.00** (a loss this week, perhaps due to the vet cost).

Seeing the loss immediately tells you to plan for a larger income next week, maybe by selling more eggs or adding a small garden product.

> **Remember:** The purpose of the log is not to be fancy; it is to give you clear, reliable numbers that you can trust when you make decisions about planting, buying supplies, or setting prices. A few minutes each day saves hours of guessing later.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It All Together: Mini Business Plan
sections.body:
Imagine you are writing a short story about your farm.  
The story has four main characters:  

* **Money plan** – how much you will spend and earn (your budget)  
* **Customers** – who will buy your produce (your market)  
* **Price tags** – how much you will charge for each item (your price)  
* **Notebook** – where you write down what happens each week (your record‑keeping)

Putting these characters together on one page makes a **mini business plan**.  
It is useful because it lets you see, at a glance, whether your farm idea can work and what you need to watch.

---

### Mini Business Plan – One‑Page Template

| Section | What to write | Example (10 m² vegetable plot) |
|---------|---------------|--------------------------------|
| **1. Farm Goal** | A short sentence describing what you will grow and why. | “Grow fresh lettuce and cherry tomatoes for the local school cafeteria.” |
| **2. Budget Summary** | List total **costs** and total **income**. Use the simple equation $$\text{Profit} = \text{Total Income} - \text{Total Costs}$$. | Costs: $150 (seeds, soil, water). Income: $300 (sale of 200 kg lettuce). Profit: $150. |
| **3. Market Choice** | Name your main customers and how you will reach them. | “School cafeteria – deliver twice a week; local farmers’ market – set up a stall on Saturdays.” |
| **4. Price Setting** | State the price per unit and how you decided it. | “Lettuce $1.50 per head, based on market price $1.30 plus $0.20 for packaging.” |
| **5. Record‑Keeping Plan** | Describe the simple log you will keep (what, when, where). | “Weekly sheet: date, amount planted, water used (litres), sales (kg and $), expenses (seed, fertilizer).” |
| **6. Risks & How to Manage Them** | List two things that could go wrong and one action for each. | “Rain damage – use row covers. Low sales – offer a discount to the school for bulk orders.” |
| **7. Next Steps** | The three immediate actions you will take after this plan. | “1) Buy seeds (by 1 Oct). 2) Contact school chef (by 5 Oct). 3) Print weekly log sheet (by 7 Oct).” |

> **Note:** *A one‑page plan is not a final contract; it is a quick check‑list that helps you stay organized and spot problems early.*

---

### How to Fill In the Template

1. **Start with the goal.** Write one clear sentence.  
   *Why?* A clear goal keeps every decision focused.  
   *Everyday comparison:* It is like setting a destination before you start a road trip.

2. **Add numbers to the budget.** List every cost you expect (seeds, tools, water) and every source of income (price × expected quantity).  
   *Why?* Numbers show whether you will make a profit.  
   *Everyday comparison:* It is the same as checking your pocket money before buying a video game.

3. **Choose your market.** Think about who will buy your food and how you will reach them.  
   *Why?* Without customers, even the best crops stay in the field.  
   *Everyday comparison:* Like deciding whether to sell lemonade to neighbors or at a school fair.

4. **Set prices.** Take the market price, add any extra cost you have, and decide a fair amount.  
   *Why?* Prices must cover costs and still be attractive to buyers.  
   *Everyday comparison:* Similar to adding a small tip to the price of a homemade cookie to cover the cost of the ingredients.

5. **Create a record‑keeping habit.** Use a simple table or notebook. Write the date, what you did, and the numbers.  
   *Why?* Records let you compare what you planned with what really happened.  
   *Everyday comparison:* Like keeping a diary of your homework scores to see where you improve.

6. **Think about risks.** Write two things that could go wrong and a quick fix for each.  
   *Why?* Planning for problems reduces surprise and loss.  
   *Everyday comparison:* Like packing an umbrella when the forecast says rain.

7. **List next steps.** Choose three actions you can do this week.  
   *Why?* Small steps keep the plan moving forward.  
   *Everyday comparison:* Like making a to‑do list for a school project.

> **Remember:** *A mini business plan is a living document.* Update it each month with real numbers and new ideas. This keeps your farm on track and helps you become a confident farmer‑entrepreneur.

sections.heading: 7. Review and Next Steps
sections.body:
Think back over everything you have just learned.  A good farm plan is like a road map: it tells you where you are now, where you want to go, and how you will get there.  By reviewing the key ideas and looking at the next steps, you can keep improving your plan and turn a tiny garden into a small, thriving farm business.

**What you should remember**

> **Remember:** A budget is a simple list of expected costs and expected income.  It helps you see if your farm will make enough money to cover what you spend.

> **In daily life:** Imagine you want to buy a new video game.  First you check how much money you have, then you add up the price of the game, any extra accessories, and the money you will still have left after the purchase.  That quick calculation is a personal budget, and the same idea works for a farm.

> **Common mistake:** Skipping the step where you write down *all* costs.  Even small items—like a bag of seed, a watering can, or a few minutes of your time—add up and can change whether your farm is profitable.

> **Definition:** *Profit* = **Income** – **Costs**.  This equation tells you how much money is left after you pay for everything.

$$
\text{Profit} = \text{Income} - \text{Costs}
$$

### 1. Check your mini‑business plan

Go through each part of the plan you created:

| Part | What to look for |
|------|------------------|
| Why a farm needs a budget | Did you explain why knowing costs matters? |
| Estimating costs and income | Are all numbers realistic? Did you use local prices? |
| Finding your market | Have you identified who will buy your produce? |
| Setting prices | Do your prices cover costs and give a reasonable profit? |
| Simple record‑keeping | Is there a place to write down daily sales and expenses? |
| Mini business plan | Does it read like a short story of “What I will do, how, and when”? |

If any box feels shaky, go back and add more detail.  A plan that feels clear now will be easier to follow later.

### 2. Try it on a small scale

The safest way to test your ideas is to start with a garden plot you already have—maybe a few raised beds in the school yard or a corner of your backyard.  Follow these steps:

1. **Pick a crop** you enjoy eating and that grows well in your climate (e.g., lettuce, radishes, or herbs).  
2. **Write a tiny budget**: list seed cost, soil amendment, water, and the time you will spend.  
3. **Estimate how much you can sell**: talk to classmates, teachers, or neighbours to see if they would buy a bunch.  
4. **Set a price** using the formula *price = (cost per unit) + desired profit per unit*.  
5. **Record every transaction** in a simple notebook or spreadsheet.  

After a few weeks you will see whether your profit estimate was right.  If you earned less than expected, look at the numbers again: maybe the seed cost was higher, or you needed more water than planned.  Adjust the budget and try again next season.

### 3. Keep improving over time

A farm plan is never finished; it grows with you.  Here are three easy ways to make it better each year:

* **Collect real data** – Write down the exact amount of water used, the actual price you paid for fertilizer, and the exact weight of each harvest.  Real numbers replace guesses.
* **Ask for feedback** – Show your record book to a teacher, a local farmer, or a family member.  They may notice a cost you missed or suggest a new market (like a school cafeteria).
* **Add one new element** – Next season, try a second crop, or experiment with a small value‑added product such as dried herbs.  Update the budget to include the new costs and potential income.

### 4. Take the next step

Now that you have practiced the whole cycle—budget, market, price, record, and review—you are ready to think bigger.  You might:

* Expand the garden area or rent a small plot of land.  
* Join a local farmers’ market to reach more customers.  
* Use simple computer tools (like a free spreadsheet) to automate calculations.  

Remember, every successful farmer started with a single seed and a simple plan.  By reviewing what you have learned, testing it on a small garden, and tweaking the numbers each year, you build confidence and skill.  Keep the cycle moving: **plan → do → record → review → improve**.  Your small farm business can grow step by step, just like the plants you tend.

examples.title: Budget for a Small Vegetable Plot
examples.given: You have 100 m² of land to grow lettuce. Seeds cost $20, fertilizer $15, and you expect to sell each head of lettuce for $2. You plan to grow 200 heads. Find the total profit.

examples.title: Pricing Tomatoes for a Local Market
examples.given: You will grow 500 kg of tomatoes. Production costs are $0.80 /kg. The local market will pay $1.20 /kg, but you want a 20 % profit margin after covering costs. Determine the price you should charge per kg.

examples.title: Mini Business Plan for a Mixed Small Farm
examples.given: You plan a 0.5 ha farm with three products: 300 m² of lettuce, 200 m² of carrots, and 100 m² of chickens (10 birds). Costs: lettuce seeds $25, carrots seed $30, chicken feed $40. Expected yields: lettuce 1.5 kg/m², carrots 2 kg/m², chickens 5 kg meat each. Sale prices: lettuce $2/kg, carrots $1.5/kg, chicken $8/kg. Find total expected profit and write a one‑sentence summary of the business viability.

steps.label: Calculate lettuce profit
steps.text: Yield = 300 m² × 1.5 kg/m² = 450 kg; revenue = 450 kg × $2 = $900; cost = $25; profit = $875.

steps.label: Calculate carrot profit
steps.text: Yield = 200 m² × 2 kg/m² = 400 kg; revenue = 400 kg × $1.5 = $600; cost = $30; profit = $570.

steps.label: Calculate chicken profit
steps.text: Yield = 10 birds × 5 kg = 50 kg; revenue = 50 kg × $8 = $400; cost = $40; profit = $360.

steps.label: Viability statement
steps.text: With an expected profit of $1,805 per season, the mixed small farm appears financially viable.

examples.answer: Total expected profit = $1,805; the farm is financially viable.

practice.q: A farmer plans to grow 100 lettuce heads. Each lettuce seed packet costs $2 and one packet plants 20 heads. How much will the seed cost?
practice.a: One packet plants 20 heads, so 100 heads ÷ 20 heads per packet = 5 packets. Each packet costs $2, so 5 × $2 = $10. The seed cost is $10.

practice.q: If the farmer expects to sell each lettuce head for $0.50, what will be the total income from the 100 heads?
practice.a: Income per head = $0.50. Total heads = 100. Multiply: 100 × $0.50 = $50. Total expected income is $50.

practice.q: The farmer’s budget includes: seeds $10, fertilizer $30, water $15, and tools $20. Estimate the total cost and calculate the profit if the expected income is $150.
practice.a: Add all costs: $10 + $30 + $15 + $20 = $75 total cost. Expected income = $150. Profit = Income – Cost = $150 – $75 = $75 profit.

practice.q: The farmer wants to sell lettuce at a local farmer’s market that charges a stall fee of $5 per day. If the market is open 3 days a week for 4 weeks, how much should the farmer add to the product price to cover the stall fees, assuming they sell 120 heads in total?
practice.a: Stall fee per day = $5. Number of days = 3 days/week × 4 weeks = 12 days. Total stall cost = $5 × 12 = $60. Total heads sold = 120. Extra amount per head = $60 ÷ 120 = $0.50. The farmer should add $0.50 to each lettuce price to cover stall fees.

practice.q: Create a simple monthly cash‑flow table for the first three months. Fixed costs: rent $200/month, utilities $50/month. Variable costs: seeds $10 (Month 1), $8 (Month 2), $12 (Month 3). Expected sales: Month 1 – 200 heads at $0.60 each; Month 2 – 250 heads at $0.55 each; Month 3 – 300 heads at $0.50 each. Show total income, total costs, and net cash flow for each month.
practice.a:
Month 1:
- Income: 200 × $0.60 = $120
- Fixed costs: $200 + $50 = $250
- Variable cost (seeds): $10
- Total cost: $250 + $10 = $260
- Net cash flow: $120 – $260 = –$140 (loss)
Month 2:
- Income: 250 × $0.55 = $137.50
- Fixed costs: $250 (same as month 1)
- Variable cost (seeds): $8
- Total cost: $250 + $8 = $258
- Net cash flow: $137.50 – $258 = –$120.50 (loss)
Month 3:
- Income: 300 × $0.50 = $150
- Fixed costs: $250
- Variable cost (seeds): $12
- Total cost: $250 + $12 = $262
- Net cash flow: $150 – $262 = –$112 (loss)

practice.q: Using the three‑month cash‑flow results above, calculate the break‑even price per head for Month 3 if the farmer can reduce fixed costs by 10 % starting Month 4 and expects to sell 350 heads that month. Show the calculation.
practice.a:
1. Reduce fixed costs by 10 %: Fixed costs originally $250 → $250 × 0.90 = $225.
2. Variable seed cost for Month 4 (assume same as Month 3) = $12.
3. Total cost for Month 4 = Fixed $225 + Variable $12 = $237.
4. Expected sales = 350 heads.
5. Break‑even price = Total cost ÷ Number of heads = $237 ÷ 350 ≈ $0.677 per head.
So the farmer needs to charge about $0.68 per lettuce head in Month 4 to break even.

recap: This lesson explains why a farm needs a budget, how to estimate costs and income, and how to find a market for farm products. It shows how to set prices that cover all costs and generate profit, and introduces simple daily record‑keeping. Finally, it combines these steps into a one‑page mini business plan to help a small farm run like a tiny business.

key_terms.meaning: A written estimate of all expected expenses and income for a set period.
A careful guess of costs or income based on available information.
Expenses that stay the same regardless of how much is produced, such as rent or loan payments.
Expenses that change with production level, like seeds, fertilizer, water, and labor.
A group of potential customers and the place where buying and selling happen.
Money left after all expenses have been paid.
Writing down daily transactions so totals can be added accurately later.
A one‑page summary that includes budget, market, pricing, and record‑keeping.

quiz.q: Why is a budget important for a small farm?
options: It tells you what you can afford and prevents surprise costs
It eliminates the need for a market
It replaces the need for record‑keeping
quiz.why: A budget shows affordable expenses and helps avoid unexpected costs.

quiz.q: What is the difference between fixed and variable costs?
options: Fixed costs change with production; variable costs stay the same
Fixed costs stay the same; variable costs change with production
Variable costs are only for labor
quiz.why: Fixed costs do not depend on output, while variable costs do.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a market for a small farm?
quiz.why: A school cafeteria represents a group of customers who could buy the farm’s produce.

quiz.q: When setting a price, the first step is to:
options: Calculate the total cost per unit
Ask friends what they think it should cost
quiz.why: You must know the total cost per unit before adding profit.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of daily record‑keeping?
options: To make it easier to add up totals later
quiz.why: Writing each transaction daily prevents reliance on memory and speeds up summarising.

quiz.q: A mini business plan helps you:
options: See at a glance if the farm idea can work
quiz.why: It combines budget, market, pricing, and records into one quick overview.
